name: S-40503

card.summary: A preclinical nonsteroidal SARM tested in rat osteoporosis models; known mainly from doping-control research, with no human efficacy data.
card.note: Preclinical only; detectable in doping tests.

quick.overview:
S-40503 is an experimental nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM). It was described in 2003 in rat models of osteoporosis, where it showed bone-building activity.

No human clinical trials are listed in the sources consulted. It is discussed mainly in anti-doping analytical literature.
quick.mechanism: It binds the androgen receptor with nanomolar affinity and preferentially over other nuclear receptors. In orchiectomized rats given it for 4 weeks, researchers evaluated its bone effects against dihydrotestosterone.
quick.risks: No human safety data are described. SARMs are prohibited by WADA, and doping-control laboratories have developed methods to detect S-40503 in human plasma.

lead: S-40503 is a nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) first described in 2003 as a compound developed to pursue tissue-selective androgen receptor activity.[1] It bound the androgen receptor with nanomolar affinity, with preference for it among nuclear receptors, and was evaluated in rat models of osteoporosis against dihydrotestosterone.[1]

Later literature on it comes mostly from doping control, where laboratories described identifying it in human plasma as an emerging drug with potential for misuse.[2][3] The sources consulted describe no human trials.

paras: No studies found. Published work is limited to rat studies of bone effects[1] and analytical doping-control methods.[2][3]
In the 2003 report, S-40503 preferentially bound the androgen receptor over other nuclear receptors, and effects on bone were assessed in orchiectomized rats treated for 4 weeks.[1]

A 2009 study developed plasma methods to identify S-40503 alongside GW501516, S-107 and JTV-519 as emerging drugs with misuse potential.[3] A 2018 review notes that SARMs have been the subject of two decades of clinical research aimed at muscle-wasting conditions and are considered a doping-relevant class.[2]

timeline.event: S-40503 reported in rat models of osteoporosis.[1]
Doping-control method for S-40503 in human plasma published.[3]
